questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: In which part of the Indian subcontinent did the Harappan civilisation mainly flourish?
questions.explanation: Its main sites lie in the north-western region and the Indus basin.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Which alloy, made of copper and tin, was used by Harappan craftspeople for tools and objects?
questions.explanation: Bronze and copper were widely used; iron was not.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Why did many Harappan settlements grow up near rivers?
options: Rivers provided water, fertile land and routes for transport
Rivers kept people away from farms
questions.explanation: Water, fertile soil and river transport all supported settlement.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Which statement about Harappan seals and script is correct?
options: The script has been fully deciphered
Seals carry short inscriptions in a script yet to be deciphered
questions.explanation: The short inscriptions on seals remain unread.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Why is comparing Harappan finds with other contemporary civilisations such as Mesopotamia useful?
options: It shows that no two civilisations existed
It proves that they were identical
It reveals similarities and differences in trade, urban life and writing
It removes the need for excavation
questions.explanation: Comparison places the Harappan civilisation in a wider context.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Differences in the size of houses at Harappan sites suggest
options: some differences in wealth or status among residents
that everyone lived in identical houses
questions.explanation: Varied house sizes hint at social differences.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Describe the economy of the Harappan civilisation.
questions.answer: The economy rested on agriculture, with crops such as wheat and barley, and on crafts such as bead making and pottery. Trade, including with distant regions, linked it to other societies.
questions.explanation: Farming, craft and trade together sustained the cities.

questions.topic: Harappan civilisation
questions.q: Why was a drainage system important in a densely populated Harappan city?
questions.answer: A drainage system carried waste water away, keeping streets and homes clean and lowering the risk of disease. Its planning also shows that the city had some organised civic arrangements.
questions.explanation: Sanitation was essential in crowded cities.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: The Lion Capital at Sarnath is the basis of
questions.explanation: The national emblem is adapted from the Sarnath capital of Ashoka's time.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Who founded the Mauryan Empire?
questions.explanation: Chandragupta Maurya founded the empire in the fourth century BCE.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: The Arthashastra mainly deals with
questions.explanation: It is a treatise on governance and economic policy.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Who deciphered the Brahmi script of Ashoka's inscriptions in the 1830s?
questions.explanation: James Prinsep's work made Ashokan inscriptions readable.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Why was the decipherment of Brahmi important to historians?
options: It proved the Harappan script was Brahmi
It allowed Ashokan and many other early inscriptions to be read
It ended the study of coins
questions.explanation: Reading Brahmi opened a large body of early records.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: What does the spread of Buddhism to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia show?
options: Ideas travelled with monks and traders, linking India with other regions
questions.explanation: Cultural exchange moved along trade and travel routes.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: Name any two Gupta rulers.
questions.answer: Chandragupta I and Samudragupta were Gupta rulers. Chandragupta II and Skandagupta are others.
questions.explanation: These rulers are well known from Gupta history.

questions.topic: Early states, Mauryan and Gupta periods, and ancient society
questions.q: What role did guilds play in the economy of ancient India?
questions.answer: Guilds organised crafts and trade, set standards and rules for members, and some also took deposits and lent money. Many guilds also supported religious institutions through donations.
questions.explanation: Guilds were important economic and social organisations.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Who wrote the Baburnama?
questions.explanation: The Baburnama is the memoir of Babur.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Who built the Red Fort at Delhi?
questions.explanation: Shah Jahan built the Red Fort when he moved his capital to Shahjahanabad.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Which Vijayanagara ruler is noted for his patronage of art and literature, and for a work in Telugu?
questions.explanation: Krishnadevaraya is remembered for his patronage and for composing Amuktamalyada.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Chaitanya was a Bhakti saint who was devoted to
questions.explanation: Chaitanya popularised Krishna bhakti in Bengal.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Why do historians read court chronicles like the Akbarnama with care?
options: They were written under royal patronage and may present the ruler favourably
questions.explanation: Patronage can shape how events are presented.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Why did Akbar's officials measure land and record its fertility?
options: To assess revenue on the basis of productivity
questions.explanation: Measurement and classification helped fix revenue on the basis of productivity.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: Mention two teachings of Kabir.
questions.answer: Kabir taught devotion to one formless God and criticised idol worship and empty ritual. He also rejected caste distinctions and urged simple, honest living.
questions.explanation: His verses stress devotion and equality.

questions.topic: Medieval India: Mughals, Vijayanagara, Bhakti and Sufi
questions.q: How did the Mughal state try to win the loyalty of regional elites?
questions.answer: It gave ranks and offices to nobles of different backgrounds, including Rajput chiefs, and formed marriage alliances with some ruling families. A policy of religious tolerance and recognition of local zamindars also helped.
keyPoints: Ranks and offices to local chiefs
questions.explanation: Inclusion helped build a stable empire.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: In which year was the English East India Company chartered?
questions.explanation: The Company received its royal charter in 1600.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Who was the Governor-General of India at the time of the 1857 revolt?
questions.explanation: Lord Canning was Governor-General during the revolt.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Which of these was a result of the Permanent Settlement?
options: Peasants became owners paying no revenue
Zamindars became hereditary landlords with a fixed revenue demand
Revenue was collected by the army
questions.explanation: Zamindars gained hereditary rights and a fixed payment.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Why did the British introduce the telegraph and postal system?
options: To strengthen administration and military control and aid trade
questions.explanation: Faster communication served administration, the army and commerce.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Why were Deccan peasants in the 1870s heavily indebted?
options: Cotton prices fell after the boom of the American Civil War years while revenue demand stayed high
questions.explanation: The fall in prices and fixed demands pushed peasants towards moneylenders.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Why did the rebels of 1857 choose Bahadur Shah Zafar as their leader?
options: He was a symbol of authority recognised by many, which gave the revolt legitimacy
questions.explanation: The Mughal emperor still had symbolic authority.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Name two social reforms of the nineteenth century linked to reformers or the government.
questions.answer: The practice of sati was banned in 1829 during William Bentinck's time, with the support of reformers such as Raja Ram Mohan Roy. The Widow Remarriage Act of 1856 followed efforts of Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.
questions.explanation: Reformers and the government acted together in these cases.

questions.topic: Colonial rule, 1857 and the countryside
questions.q: Evaluate the effects of the railways on India's economy under British rule.
questions.answer: Railways joined markets and moved raw materials to ports, helping trade and also famine relief. However, they mainly served British commercial and military needs, and much of the benefit went to Britain.
keyPoints: Helped movement of goods and relief
questions.explanation: The effects were mixed.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Who is called the Father of the Nation in India?
questions.explanation: Gandhi is widely called the Father of the Nation.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: The Dandi March ended at Dandi in which present-day state?
questions.explanation: Dandi is a coastal village in Gujarat.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: The Khilafat Movement was launched to
options: protest against the treatment of the Ottoman Caliph after the First World War
questions.explanation: It was a movement of Indian Muslims over the Caliph's position.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Which agreement of 1916 was made between the Congress and the Muslim League?
questions.explanation: The Lucknow Pact of 1916 brought the two organisations together.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Why did Gandhi prefer the term satyagraha to passive resistance?
options: He stressed the force of truth and active non-violent resistance
questions.explanation: Satyagraha means holding on to truth, an active moral force.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Why did the Congress ministries of 1937 matter in the national movement?
options: They gave up the goal of swaraj
They showed that Indians could run provincial governments, building confidence in self-rule
questions.explanation: Experience of office strengthened confidence in self-government.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: Mention two constructive programmes promoted by Gandhi.
questions.answer: Gandhi promoted khadi and spinning to encourage self-reliance. He also worked for the removal of untouchability and for harmony among communities.
questions.explanation: Constructive work complemented political struggle.

questions.topic: Gandhi and the national movement
questions.q: How did newspapers in Indian languages help spread nationalist ideas?
questions.answer: They carried news and criticism of British policies to people who did not read English. They helped create public opinion, which is why the government tried to control them, as in the Vernacular Press Act of 1878.
questions.explanation: The press was an important means of spreading ideas.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: How many groups of Fundamental Rights does the Constitution now guarantee?
questions.explanation: There are six groups of Fundamental Rights.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: In which year did the Constituent Assembly first meet?
questions.explanation: It first met in December 1946.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Which event of 30 January 1948 deeply shocked the nation?
options: The end of the Constituent Assembly
questions.explanation: Gandhi was assassinated in New Delhi on that date.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: In which part of the Constitution are the Directive Principles of State Policy found?
questions.explanation: Part IV contains the Directive Principles.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Why did many leaders favour a secular state in India after Partition?
options: To ensure equal citizenship for all communities in a country of many faiths
questions.explanation: A secular state gives equal citizenship regardless of religion.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Article 1 describes India as a Union of States. What did this wording stress?
options: States may leave the Union freely
The Union is indestructible and states cannot secede
questions.explanation: The framers stressed that the Union cannot be broken up by the states.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: What does the word sovereign in the Preamble mean?
questions.answer: Sovereign means that India is fully independent and has supreme authority over its own affairs. It is not subject to the control of any outside power.
questions.explanation: It is the first of the Preamble's descriptions of the state.

questions.topic: Partition, Independence and the Constitution
questions.q: Why was it significant that the Constitution was drafted by a Constituent Assembly of Indians and not by the British Parliament?
questions.answer: It meant that Indians themselves framed the rules of their government, which gave the Constitution legitimacy. The members, chosen mainly by the provincial assemblies, represented many regions and views.
questions.explanation: Self-made rules gave the Constitution democratic authority.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: The Parliament of India consists of the President and
options: the Supreme Court and the Cabinet
questions.explanation: The President and the two Houses form Parliament.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: What is the minimum voting age for Lok Sabha elections?
questions.explanation: The voting age was lowered to 18 by the 61st Amendment.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: Which Article makes education a Fundamental Right for children aged 6 to 14?
questions.explanation: Article 21A, inserted in 2002, provides this right.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: A Bill becomes an Act after
options: passing both Houses and receiving the President's assent
being read once in the Lok Sabha
questions.explanation: Both Houses must pass it and the President must give assent.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: Why are Fundamental Rights subject to reasonable restrictions?
options: To balance individual freedom with public order, security and the rights of others
questions.explanation: One person's freedom must be compatible with others' rights and public order.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: Why does the stability of a coalition government depend on its partners?
options: One party always has a majority
No single party has a majority, so the government relies on allied parties for support
questions.explanation: A coalition survives only as long as partners support it.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: State two functions of the Election Commission of India.
questions.answer: The Election Commission conducts free and fair elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. It also prepares electoral rolls and enforces the Model Code of Conduct.
keyPoints: Enforces the Model Code of Conduct
questions.explanation: It is an independent constitutional body under Article 324.

questions.topic: Indian political system: rights, Parliament, judiciary, federalism
questions.q: How do the legislature, executive and judiciary act as checks on one another?
questions.answer: The legislature makes laws and holds the executive accountable through questions and votes. The executive carries out laws and can be questioned in courts, while the judiciary can strike down laws or actions that violate the Constitution.
keyPoints: Legislature makes laws and holds the executive accountable
questions.explanation: Separation of functions with mutual checks protects against misuse of power.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Why was the Cold War called cold?
options: It was fought in cold regions only
It was fought only in winter
There was no direct large-scale war between the two superpowers
questions.explanation: The rivalry was fought through alliances, arms races and indirect conflicts.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Which of these is a United Nations agency dealing with health?
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization is a UN specialised agency.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: The Bandung Conference of 1955 brought together
options: newly independent Asian and African countries
questions.explanation: It was a meeting of Asian and African countries, many newly independent.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Which of these is an international financial institution set up after the Second World War?
questions.explanation: The World Bank was created in the Bretton Woods arrangements of 1944.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Why are General Assembly resolutions generally not binding on states?
options: They are recommendations rather than enforceable orders
They are written by the Secretariat alone
questions.explanation: The Assembly's resolutions carry moral and political weight but are generally not legally binding.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: Why did several European Union members adopt a common currency, the euro?
options: To lower the number of countries
To ease trade and deepen economic integration
questions.explanation: A common currency removes exchange-rate costs among members.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: What was the Berlin Wall and what did its fall in 1989 symbolise?
questions.answer: The Berlin Wall divided East and West Berlin from 1961. Its fall in 1989 symbolised the end of the division of Europe and the approaching end of the Cold War.
keyPoints: Symbol of the end of Cold War divisions
questions.explanation: The wall became a symbol of the Cold War division.

questions.topic: World politics: Cold War, UN and regional organisations
questions.q: How did the formation of the European Union reflect the idea of integration after the Second World War?
questions.answer: After the destruction of the war, European countries sought to prevent future conflict through economic cooperation, beginning with joint control of coal and steel in the early 1950s. This grew into a common market and later the Union with shared institutions.
keyPoints: Started with coal and steel cooperation
Grew into a common market and Union
questions.explanation: Economic cooperation was used to build peace.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: The process by which a growing share of people live in towns and cities is called
questions.explanation: Urbanisation is the increase in the share of urban population.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: People who move with their animals from place to place in search of pasture are called
questions.explanation: Pastoral nomads depend on herding and move seasonally.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: The dependency ratio is the ratio of
options: the young and old to the working-age population
the rural to the urban population
questions.explanation: It compares dependants with the working-age group.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Which of these regions in India is generally densely populated?
questions.explanation: Fertile soil and water support dense settlement in the Ganga plain.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Why do many large cities develop along rivers or coasts?
options: Water, trade routes and a fertile hinterland support large populations
questions.explanation: Water and transport links support commerce and settlement.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Why is the education of girls often linked with lower birth rates?
options: Education has no effect on families
Education, especially of women, is often linked with later marriage and smaller families
questions.explanation: Studies commonly find that more education for women is linked with smaller families.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Describe two characteristics of rural settlements.
questions.answer: Most people in rural settlements depend on agriculture and related primary activities. Settlements are usually small, with fewer services, and are closely tied to land and local resources.
keyPoints: Dependence on agriculture or primary activities
questions.explanation: Rural economies are based mainly on the land.

questions.topic: Geography: population and human settlements
questions.q: Why do young people from some rural regions move to cities?
questions.answer: Rural areas may offer few jobs outside farming and limited schools and health services. Cities offer wider employment and better facilities, so these push and pull factors lead to migration.
keyPoints: Better jobs and services in cities
questions.explanation: Rural-to-urban migration is driven by opportunity gaps.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Which of these is a metallic mineral?
questions.explanation: Iron ore is a metallic mineral.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Which source of energy comes from the heat of the Earth's interior?
questions.explanation: Geothermal energy uses heat from within the Earth.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Which kind of farming uses large landholdings, machinery and chemicals mainly to grow crops for sale?
questions.explanation: Commercial farming is market-oriented and capital-intensive.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: What is humus?
options: The organic part of soil formed from decayed plants and animals
A type of fertiliser made of salt
questions.explanation: Humus makes soil fertile.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Why is the jute industry concentrated in the lower Ganga basin?
options: Jute is grown in the region, and river transport and the Kolkata port help
questions.explanation: Raw material and transport links favour the region.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: A farmer in a dry region wants to save water while irrigating. Which method suits best?
questions.explanation: Drip irrigation delivers small amounts of water directly to plant roots.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: Differentiate between renewable and non-renewable resources, with an example of each.
questions.answer: Renewable resources, such as solar energy or wind, are replenished naturally and are not exhausted by use. Non-renewable resources, such as coal or petroleum, take millions of years to form and can be used up.
questions.explanation: The difference lies in how quickly a resource is replenished.

questions.topic: Geography: resources, agriculture and industry
questions.q: How does agriculture contribute to industrial development?
questions.answer: Agriculture supplies raw materials such as cotton, jute and sugarcane to industries. It also provides a market for industrial goods such as fertilisers and machinery and gives employment to many people.
questions.explanation: Farming and industry are closely linked.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Which mode of transport is the fastest?
questions.explanation: Air transport is the fastest mode.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Which of these is an Indian satellite system used for communication?
questions.explanation: INSAT is India's communication satellite system.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Which roads link state capitals, major ports and industrial centres and are maintained by the Central Government?
questions.explanation: National Highways form the main road network across states.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Which of these is an invisible item of trade?
questions.explanation: Services such as tourism are invisible items because they are not physical goods.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Under what condition can a country's HDI rise even if its income stays the same?
options: When literacy and life expectancy fall
When life expectancy and education improve
questions.explanation: HDI also depends on health and education.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Why do natural harbours help in the development of ports?
options: They are far from the sea
Deep sheltered water allows ships to dock safely with less dredging
questions.explanation: Natural depth and shelter reduce construction costs.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: State two benefits of mobile and internet connectivity for rural areas.
questions.answer: Connectivity gives farmers and workers quick access to information such as weather and market prices. It also makes services such as banking and education easier to reach.
questions.explanation: Connectivity reduces distance as a barrier.

questions.topic: Geography: transport, trade and human development
questions.q: Why is transport called the lifeline of an economy?
questions.answer: Transport moves raw materials to factories and goods to markets, and moves people to work. It links production and consumption and helps all regions to develop.
questions.explanation: Without transport, trade and production would not be connected.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: Land, labour, capital and enterprise are known as
questions.explanation: These are the four factors of production.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: Which of these is a commercial bank?
questions.explanation: The State Bank of India is a commercial bank.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: In the expenditure approach, household spending on goods and services is called
questions.explanation: GDP expenditure = consumption + investment + government spending + net exports.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: The repo rate is the rate at which
options: the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks
questions.explanation: Repo is the RBI's short-term lending rate to banks.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: Nominal GDP grows by 10 per cent while prices rise by 6 per cent. Real GDP growth is roughly
questions.explanation: Real growth is about nominal growth minus inflation, that is 10 - 6 = 4 per cent.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: Why is saving called a leakage in the circular flow of income?
options: Income that is saved is not spent on domestic goods, so it leaves the flow unless invested
questions.explanation: Savings reduce the flow of spending unless they are channelled into investment.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: Differentiate between demand deposits and time deposits.
questions.answer: Demand deposits can be withdrawn on demand without notice, as in current accounts. Time deposits are kept for a fixed period, as in fixed deposits, and usually earn higher interest.
keyPoints: Demand deposits withdrawn at any time
Time deposits for a fixed period
questions.explanation: The two differ in liquidity.

questions.topic: Economics: national income, money and banking
questions.q: How can inflation hurt people with fixed incomes?
questions.answer: When prices rise, a fixed income buys fewer goods, so purchasing power falls. Savings held as money also lose value, so people on fixed incomes find it harder to meet needs.
questions.explanation: A fixed income cannot adjust to rising prices.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Which tax is imposed on goods brought into the country from abroad?
questions.explanation: Customs duty is levied on imports.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: The Five-Year Plans in India were prepared by the
questions.explanation: The Planning Commission prepared the Five-Year Plans.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: If a budget deficit is financed by borrowing, it adds to
questions.explanation: Borrowing increases the government's debt.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Which sector received priority in the First Five-Year Plan?
questions.explanation: The First Plan stressed agriculture and irrigation.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: Why did the Second Five-Year Plan stress heavy industry?
options: To build an industrial base and reduce dependence on imported capital goods
questions.explanation: The aim was to build capital goods industries and self-reliance.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: A rising share of services in GDP over time indicates
options: a shift of the economy from agriculture towards industry and services
questions.explanation: The shift is a typical sign of structural change as an economy develops.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: State two objectives of the Five-Year Plans.
questions.answer: The plans aimed at economic growth and at self-reliance in production. They also sought to reduce poverty and inequality.
questions.explanation: These were the main stated goals of planning.

questions.topic: Economics: budget, external sector and development since 1991
questions.q: How does a depreciation of the rupee affect an importer and an exporter?
questions.answer: A depreciation raises the rupee price of imported goods, so an importer pays more. For an exporter, foreign buyers find the goods cheaper in dollars and the exporter earns more rupees per dollar, which can help sales.
keyPoints: Exports become cheaper for foreign buyers
Exporter earns more rupees per dollar
questions.explanation: A weaker rupee raises import costs and helps exporters.
